result:
I keep thinking about the Museum of Small Things.

It doesn't exist, of course. Not really. If you looked it up on a map, you wouldn't find it. But I have a very clear picture of it in my mind, and I visit it often.

The entrance is unremarkable. It's on a side street that you only find because you took a wrong turn on the way to somewhere else. The door is heavy wood, the kind that swells a little in the summer so you have to push hard with your shoulder. There's a bell that jingles, not an electronic chime, but an actual brass bell on a spring. Inside, it smells like old paper and lemon cleaner and faintly of rain, even when it hasn't rained.

There is no front desk. There's just a woman with gray hair in a cardigan sitting on a stool, reading a book. She doesn't look up when you come in, but she says, "Take your time," in a way that makes you feel like you actually have time to take.

The museum is one long room. No wings, no floors. Just one room with high windows that let in that milky, northern light that doesn't cast sharp shadows. And along the walls are shelves. Hundreds of shelves from floor to ceiling, and each shelf holds small things.

Not important things. Not crown jewels or dinosaur bones or moon rocks. Small things.

Shelf one: Buttons. Not a collection of rare, antique buttons, but the lost ones. The extra button that comes sewn into the tag of a new coat that you cut off and put in a junk drawer and never see again. The button from your father's winter coat that fell off in the parking lot in 1998. The cheap plastic buttons from a child's Halloween costume. Each one in a tiny glass jar with a handwritten label.

This is the whole premise of the museum. It is a museum for things that were never meant to be remembered, but were.

There is a shelf of single earrings. A shelf of grocery lists found in carts. "eggs, milk, bread, cat food - not the fishy kind!!!" written in hurried blue ink. There's a shelf of ticket stubs that were torn just slightly too short by the usher, so the title of the movie is missing. There's a shelf of bent paperclips.

I think about this place because I think modern life has a resolution problem.

Our cameras shoot in 8K now. We can zoom into a concert from the back row and count the singer's eyelashes. Our phones record every single day, every meal, every run, every thought we make into a post. We have more memory than any generation before us. Terabytes of it. Cloud storage that promises we'll never forget anything ever again.

But we forgot how to look at low resolution.

We forgot the texture of things that happen in between the high-definition moments. The famous writer Annie Dillard once said, "How we spend our days is, of course, how we spend our lives." And our days are not made of weddings and graduations and promotions. Those are maybe twelve days in total. Our days are made of waiting for the microwave to finish. Of picking a piece of lint off a sweater. Of noticing that the neighbor's cat sits in the exact same square of sun every day at 3:14 PM.

The Museum of Small Things is an argument that those lint-picking moments are not filler. They *are* the substance.

I went for a walk yesterday with no headphones, which feels like a radical act now. I left my phone in my pocket. And because my hands had nothing to do and my ears had nothing to listen to, my eyes had to work overtime. 

I saw how many different shades of green there are in just one block. There is the almost-yellow green of new leaves, and the deep, waxy green of the holly bush that never dies, and the dusty green of a car that someone hasn't washed since spring. I saw a man trying to parallel park a much too large truck into a much too small space, and the way he stuck his tongue out slightly in concentration, the way my brother used to when he was doing math homework.

I heard a conversation between two women ahead of me, only a fragment: "...and I told her, that's not how you make potato salad," with such profound, offended dignity that I had to stop myself from laughing out loud.

None of this will go on Instagram. None of this is content. It can't be monetized or turned into a carousel post titled "5 Mindful Moments From My Walk." It was just... there. And then it was gone.

Maybe that's why we feel so tired all the time. We are trying to archive a river.

We treat our brains like hard drives that need to be backed up constantly. If we don't photograph the coffee, did we drink it? If we don't journal the insight, did we have it? We are terrified that something will be lost. So we keep everything. And when you keep everything, you have a hoarder's house, not a museum. You can't move.

The art of a museum is not in what it keeps. It's in what it chooses to leave out. Curation is an act of love and violence. You say: This matters enough to be placed under glass. This does not.

The Museum of Small Things in my head is so peaceful because its curator was so specific. She only collected things that everyone else agreed were worthless. She looked at the giant, screaming world of Important Things and said, no, thank you. I'm going to keep the bread tags.

I think we need to become better curators of our own lives.

When I was a kid, my grandmother had a junk drawer. Every house had one then. It was usually in the kitchen. It wasn't junk, actually. It was a museum. It had rubber bands from bundles of asparagus, a single birthday candle, a takeout menu from a place that closed in 2005, batteries of uncertain charge, a tiny screwdriver you get for free when you buy reading glasses. You would open it looking for tape and you would stay for ten minutes, just sifting.

We don't have junk drawers anymore. We have search bars. If you want tape, you order tape and it arrives tomorrow. We optimized the junk away. And we lost the ten minutes of sifting.

I worry sometimes that we are losing our ability to sift altogether. To tolerate ambiguity and unlabeled things. Every app wants to categorize us, to predict us, to file us neatly. Are you a minimalist? A foodie? An entrepreneur? But most people are a messy, beautiful junk drawer. You can be someone who loves death metal and also cries at dog food commercials. You can be deeply ambitious and also want to lie on the floor for an hour.

The small things allow for that contradiction. A paperclip doesn't need to be anything more than a paperclip.

So here is my proposal, for whoever reads this: build your own small museum. Not on a shelf. In your head.

Today, collect three small things that no one will ever ask you about again.

Notice the way the light hits the dust in your kitchen at 4 p.m. Notice the exact sound your front door makes when it clicks shut - every door has a different click, and you know yours so well you could identify it blindfolded. Notice how your co-worker always says "yup, yup, yup" quickly when they're trying to get off the phone.

Put them in jars. Label them in your mind.

You don't have to write them down. You don't have to share them. In fact, it's better if you don't.

Let them be unpaid, unrecorded, unoptimized. Let them be small.

Because in fifty years, you won't remember what your inbox looked like on May 13th, 2026. You won't remember the trending audio or the viral take. But you might, if you're lucky and if you practiced, remember the way the rain smelled on that Tuesday afternoon when you had nowhere to be.

And that will be enough. That will be everything.

The woman at the entrance of my museum is still reading. She turns a page. Outside, it finally starts to rain for real.
